\section{Purpose}

This note fixes terminology for a recurring failure mode in the formalization
of the low individual degree test paper, \path{arXiv:2009.12982}.  It
complements the note-writing policy in \path{docs/paper-gaps/policy.tex} and
the source-statement audit tracked historically in \ghissue{1458}.  The current
source-boundary proof holes are tracked in \ghissue{1507} and \ghissue{422}.
A proof may be blocked at
an intermediate mathematical assertion.  If that assertion is added as a new
hypothesis to a theorem labelled as a paper theorem, the resulting \Lean{}
theorem
may be correct as a conditional statement, but it is no longer the theorem in
the cited source.  The apparent proof has not closed the paper theorem; it has
moved a proof obligation into the theorem statement.

The protocol below distinguishes such proof debt from legitimate formal
boundary conditions and from genuine mathematical corrections.  It is meant for
contributors and reviewers who must decide whether a bridge, residual, repair,
input, or obligation structure is a proved local construction, a tracked proof
gap, or statement drift which must be repaired before a theorem may be
advertised as a source theorem.  The default rule is restrictive: such data
must not be added to a paper-facing theorem unless it is part of the cited
source statement or a documented faithful encoding of its ambient hypotheses.

\section{Basic objects}

\paragraph{Source theorem.}
A source theorem is a theorem, lemma, proposition, or corollary in the paper
source under \path{references/ldt-paper/}.  Its hypotheses and conclusion are
the mathematical ground truth, subject only to faithful formal encoding and to
documented paper-gap corrections.

\paragraph{Paper-facing declaration.}
A \Lean{} declaration is paper-facing when it is named or cited as the
formalization of a source theorem, for instance through a blueprint
\verb|\lean{}| link on a theorem environment carrying a paper label.  Such a
declaration must match the source theorem in its public statement.  In
particular, it may not add an unproved bridge, residual, repair, input,
obligation structure, or other proof-obligation hypothesis which the paper does
not assume.

\paragraph{Proof obligation.}
A proof obligation is an intermediate assertion needed by the proof of a source
theorem.  It may be a construction, an estimate, a transport lemma, or a
comparison between two formal representations.  If the paper proves or invokes
this assertion, then the formalization should state it as a separate lemma or
theorem and prove it from the upstream hypotheses.

\paragraph{Obligation discharger.}
An obligation discharger is a theorem or definition which constructs a proof
obligation from the paper hypotheses already available at that point in the
argument.  This is the preferred representation of missing work.  If the proof
is not yet complete, the discharger may temporarily contain a tracked
\verb|sorry|, but the paper-facing theorem should call it rather than assume
its output as an additional theorem hypothesis.

\paragraph{Conditional helper.}
A conditional helper is a separately named theorem whose statement explicitly
assumes a proof obligation.  Names such as
\leanid{mainFormal\_ofInternalObligations},
\leanid{orthonormalization\_ofInput}, or names whose suffix advertises the
assumed obligation are permitted only when the declaration is not presented as
the source theorem.  A conditional helper is a quarantine for downstream proof
content; it does not close the source theorem.

\section{Bridge, residual, repair, input, and obligation structures}

The words \emph{bridge}, \emph{residual}, \emph{repair}, \emph{input}, and
\emph{obligation structure} name possible formal shapes.  They become dangerous
when their mathematical status is unclear or when their names make unproved
data look like acceptable hypotheses of a source theorem.

\paragraph{Bridge.}
A bridge should be a transport theorem between two already defined
mathematical forms: for example, a tensor-placement identity, a conversion
between two equivalent consistency relations, or a statement translating a
source object into a formal representation.  A bridge is harmless only after it
is proved from previously available assumptions.  It becomes proof debt when it
is assumed because the transport has not yet been proved.  It becomes theorem
drift when the assumed bridge is added to a paper-facing theorem.

\paragraph{Residual.}
A residual is a named remainder after part of an argument has been performed.
It is often a useful way to record the exact missing target after a completed
construction.  A residual may appear as the conclusion of a helper theorem or
as the input of a quarantined conditional helper.  It is not a permissible new
assumption on a paper theorem unless the paper itself assumes that residual.

\paragraph{Input.}
An input is a named bundle of data or hypotheses consumed by a construction or
conditional helper.  It is harmless only when each load-bearing field is either
part of the source hypotheses or is produced by an earlier theorem.  It becomes
proof debt when the bundle is merely assumed because the construction of its
fields is missing.  It becomes theorem drift when such a bundle is added to the
public statement of a source theorem.

\paragraph{Repair.}
A repair is a mathematical construction which replaces an approximate or
partial object by a better object, usually with a quantitative estimate.  In
the low individual degree test formalization, projectivization and
orthonormalization repairs are genuine mathematical operations.  A repair
should therefore appear as a construction or as a theorem discharging the
corresponding obligation.  If a theorem assumes the output of the repair instead
of constructing it, that theorem is conditional on the repair.

\paragraph{Obligation structure.}
An obligation structure is a record whose fields are the data and estimates
needed by a later construction.  This is acceptable only as an internal target
or as a hypothesis of a conditional helper.  Such a structure becomes statement
drift if it is added to a paper-facing theorem instead of being constructed
inside the proof.  The review question is whether every load-bearing field is
proved from the source hypotheses or is explicitly tracked as a missing
obligation.

\section{The main failure mode}

Suppose the paper proves
\[
  H \Longrightarrow C.
\]
During formalization, the proof may need an intermediate assertion \(B\).  The
paper theorem should be represented as
\[
  H \Longrightarrow B \Longrightarrow C
  \quad\text{inside the proof,}
\]
where \(B\) is obtained by a lemma or theorem from \(H\).  The following
public statement is a different theorem:
\[
  H \land B \Longrightarrow C.
\]
It is not unsound in \Lean{}, but it is not the paper theorem.  It says that the
conclusion follows if the missing bridge data is supplied.  Such a theorem is a
conditional helper, even if its conclusion looks exactly like the paper's
conclusion.

This is the situation colloquially described as ``adding a bridge
hypothesis''.  More precisely, an unproved intermediate step has been promoted
from the proof body to the theorem's assumptions.  The correction is not to hide
the hypothesis under a different structure name.  The correction is to keep a
paper-facing theorem with the source statement and move the missing step to a
named internal proof obligation.

\section{Faithful boundary hypotheses}

Not every extra formal hypothesis is a theorem drift.  Some hypotheses are
faithful boundary conditions introduced by formal encoding.  Examples include
nonnegativity needed for a real power, positivity needed to divide by a
quantity, finiteness and nonemptiness of an index type, a field-model instance,
or decidability instances required by \Lean{}.  Such hypotheses are acceptable
when they express part of the mathematical ambient setting or make explicit a
condition used implicitly in the paper.

The distinction is load-bearing.  A faithful boundary hypothesis describes the
domain in which the paper's objects live.  A proof-debt hypothesis supplies a
mathematical step that the proof should derive.  If removing the hypothesis
leaves an unproved construction or estimate from the paper proof, then the
hypothesis is proof debt, not a boundary condition.

\section{Definition drift and subtree repair}

Definition drift is especially dangerous because it propagates.  If a
definition is changed so that it no longer denotes the object in the paper,
then every downstream theorem using that definition may continue to compile
while proving statements about the wrong object.  Downstream theorem statements
can then be repaired piecemeal, but the development remains unstable because
the wrong definition is still upstream.

When a definition mismatch is found, the repair should proceed by a subtree
protocol.

\begin{enumerate}
  \item Identify the source object and the formal object precisely.
  \item Freeze a source-faithful definition or state an adapter theorem
  relating the existing definition to the source object.
  \item Recheck the downstream theorem chain against that definition or adapter.
  \item Re-formalize the affected subtree from the corrected interface, rather
  than adding local hypotheses to each downstream theorem.
  \item If a downstream proof cannot be completed, record the missing obligation
  at the lowest point where the paper proof needs it.
\end{enumerate}

This is slower than editing a final theorem signature, but it prevents a local
definition error from becoming a global theorem-statement error.

\section{Allowed shapes}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{p{0.24\linewidth}p{0.31\linewidth}p{0.32\linewidth}}
\textbf{Shape} & \textbf{Allowed use} & \textbf{Forbidden use} \\
\hline
Paper-facing theorem & Matches the source statement up to faithful encoding &
Carries non-paper bridge, residual, repair, input, obligation-structure, or
proof-obligation hypotheses \\
Source-shaped theorem with a tracked \verb|sorry| & Default repair when the
source proof is blocked but the statement is known & Replaced by a strengthened
theorem statement merely to keep the file compiling \\
Conditional helper & Temporary quarantine for substantial proof content whose
remaining named obligation has not yet been discharged & Introduced merely to
avoid a \verb|sorry|, or linked as the source theorem or marked as
proof-complete for that theorem \\
Obligation discharger theorem & Constructs the obligation from paper hypotheses &
Merely restates the obligation as an assumption \\
Input bundle & Collects produced data for a local construction & Is assumed by a
source theorem instead of being produced \\
Obligation structure & Bundles constructed data and estimates & Hides unproved
fields that are then assumed by a source theorem \\
Paper-gap note & Documents a real mathematical or formal-statement divergence &
Justifies silent statement drift without a repair plan
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\section{Protocol for a blocked proof}

When a source-labelled proof is blocked, use the following order.

\begin{enumerate}
  \item Read the cited source statement and the proof passage in
  \path{references/ldt-paper/}.
  \item Write the paper theorem form, the current \Lean{} theorem form, and the
  first missing intermediate assertion.
  \item Decide whether the missing assertion is a faithful boundary condition,
  a representation adapter, an ordinary lemma from the paper proof, or a real
  paper-gap discrepancy.
  \item If it is an ordinary lemma or adapter, create a named theorem which
  discharges that obligation.  Do not add it to the source theorem as a new
  hypothesis.
  \item Keep the source-labelled theorem itself in the source form, even if its

   102	\paragraph{Axis-parallel lines and diagonal lines.}
   103	Before presenting a formal description of the game $\game^\ld$, we first define
   104	what we mean by lines, and their properties.
   105	
   106	\begin{definition}[Lines]
   107	  \label{def:line}
   108		A \emph{line} $\line$ in $\F^m_q$ specified by a pair $(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$
   109	  is the subset
   110	  \begin{equation}
   111	    \label{eq:line-set}
   112	    \line(u,v) = \bigl\{\, u + tv : t \in \F_q \,\bigr\} \subseteq \F_q^m \;.
   113	  \end{equation}
   114	  We call the vector $v$ a \emph{direction} of line
   115	  $\line(u,v)$.\footnote{For convenience we explicitly allow
   116	    $v=0$, in which case the line is reduced to a singleton.}
   117	  
   118	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{axis-parallel} if there is a coordinate $i \in
   119	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ for which $v$ is equal to $e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis
   120	  vector in $\F_q^m$.
   121	  We say that such a line $\line$ is \emph{parallel to the $i$-th direction}.
   122	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{diagonal} if there exists an $i \in
   123	  \{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}$ for which $v_1 = v_2 = \cdots = v_i = 0$.
   124	\end{definition}
   125	
   126	The following Proposition establishes that, for a fixed direction, a line
   127	$\line$ is an equivalence class of points on the line.
   128	\begin{proposition}
   129	  \label{prop:line-equiv}
   130	  Let $u,v \in \F_q^m$.
   131	  Then for all $u' \in \line(u,v)$, we have that $\line(u,v) = \line(u',v)$.
   132	\end{proposition}
   133	\begin{proof}
   134		Fix $u' \in \line(u,v)$.
   135	  We have that $u' = u + tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$.
   136	  Let $a \in \line(u,v)$.
   137	  This means that $a = u + sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$.
   138	  We also have that $a = u + (s - t + t)v = u + tv + (s - t)v = u' + (s - t)v$,
   139	  so $\line(u,v) \subseteq \line(u',v)$.
   140	  A similar argument shows that $\line(u',v) \subseteq \line(u,v)$.
   141	\end{proof}
   142	
   143	We now specify a canonical representation of lines $\line = \line(u,v)$ as pairs $(u_0,v)$
   144	where $u_0$ is a \emph{canonical representative} of $\line$ specified as
   145	follows.
   146	Let $L_v^{\lnf}: \F_q^m \to \F_q^m$ denote the canonical linear map with the
   147	one-dimensional kernel basis $\{v\}$ (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical} for a
   148	definition of canonical linear map).
   149	Note that for all $u \in \line$, we have that $L_v^{\lnf}(u)$ is a point in
   150	$\line$.
   151	This is because since the image and kernel of $L_v^{\lnf}$ are complementary
   152	subspaces by definition (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical}), any $u \in \F_q^m$ has a
   153	unique decomposition $u = u_0 + u_1$ where $u_0$ is in the image of $L_v^{\lnf}$
   154	and $u_1 \in \ker(L_v^{\lnf})$, which by definition is the subspace spanned by
   155	$v$.
   156	Thus $u_1 = tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$ and we have that $u_0 = u - tv \in \line$.
   157	In particular, if $u\in \line$ then $u_0 = L_v^{\lnf}(u) \in \line$ as well. 
   158	Furthermore, since $L_v^{\lnf}$ is a projection onto its image by definition, we
   159	have $L_v^{\lnf}(u_0) = u_0$.
   160	
   161	Next, note that for any $u,u' \in \line$, since $u-u' = sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$
   162	it follows that $L_v^\lnf(u) = L_v^\lnf(u')$.
   163	Thus $u_0 = u_0'$ and this shows that $L_v^\lnf$ gives a means to compute a
   164	canonical representative of lines.
   165	
   166	\begin{definition}[Canonical representative of a line]
   167	  \label{def:line-representative}
   168	  Let $\line$ be a line in direction $v$.
   169	  A canonical representative of $\line$ is the point $u_0 \in \F_q^m$ such that
   170	  \[
   171	    u_0 = L_v^\lnf(u)
   172	  \]
   173	  for all $u \in \line$.
   174	\end{definition}

   394	We define a special class of measurements that are relevant to the soundness
   395	properties of the low-degree test.
   396	
   397	\begin{definition}[Low-degree polynomial measurements]
   398	  \label{def:ld-meas}
   399	  Define $\polymeas{m}{d}{q}$ to be the set of POVM measurements whose outcomes
   400	  correspond to (individual) degree-$d$ polynomials of $m$ variables over
   401	  $\F_q$.
   402	  More generally, for an integer $\ldc$ and tuples $m=(m_1, m_2, \ldots,
   403	  m_\ldc)$, $d=(d_1, d_2, \ldots, d_\ldc)$ and $q=(q_1, q_2, \ldots, q_\ldc)$,
   404	  we let $\simulpolymeas{m}{d}{q}{\ldc}$ be the set of measurements $G =
   405	  \{G_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots\,,\, g_\ldc}\}$ such that for $i\in\{1, 2, \ldots,
   406	  \ldc\}$, $g_i$ is a polynomial $g_i:\F_{q_i}^{m_i} \rightarrow
   407	  \F_{q_i}$ with individual degree $d_i$ (see \Cref{sec:ld-encoding} for a definition of individual degree). 
   408	\end{definition}
   409	
   410	Quantum soundness of a version of the classical low-degree test for polynomials of low \emph{total} degree was claimed
   411	in~\cite{natarajan2018low}, building on an analysis of a three-prover version of the test in~\cite{vidick2016three}. Unfortunately there is a gap in the soundness analysis of this test. For our construction we use the low individual degree test, whose quantum soundness is shown in~\cite{ML20} and generalized in~\cite{ji2021quantum}. We state the result in the form that is most directly useful for us, and show how the stated result follows from~\cite{ji2021quantum}.
   412	
   413	\begin{theorem}[Quantum soundness of the simultaneous classical low-degree test]
   414	  \label{lem:ld-soundness}
   415	  There exists a function $\delta_{\ld}(\eps, q, m, d, \ldc) = a (dm \ldc)^a (\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})$ for universal constants $a\geq 1$ and $0<b\leq 1$ 
   416	such that the following
   417	  holds.
   418	  For all $\eps > 0$ and parameter tuple $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$, for all
   419	  projective strategies $(\psi,A,B)$ that succeed with probability at least
   420	  $1-\eps$ in the game $\game^\ld_\ldparams$, there exists measurements
   421	  \[G^w \in \simulpolymeas{m}{d}{q}{\ldc}\] on $\mH_w$, for
   422	  $w\in\{\alice,\bob\}$, such that
   423	  \begin{equation*}
   424	    \begin{split}
   425	      A^{\Point,\, u}_{a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots\,,\, a_\ldc}
   426	      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
   427	      G^\bob_{[(g_1(u),g_2(u),\ldots,g_\ldc(u)) = (a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots \,,\, a_\ldc)]}\;,\\
   428	      G^\alice_{[(g_1(u),g_2(u),\ldots,g_\ldc(u)) = (a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots \,,\, a_\ldc)]}
   429	      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
   430				 B^{\Point,\, u}_{a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots\,,\, a_\ldc}\;,\\
   431	      G^\alice_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots \,,\, g_\ldc}
   432	      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
   433	      G^\bob_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots \,,\, g_\ldc}\;,
   434	    \end{split}
   435	  \end{equation*}
   436	  where $\delta_{\ld} = \delta_{\ld}(\eps, q, m, d, \ldc)$, 
   437	  and all three statements are with respect to the state $\ket{\psi}$.
   438	In addition, the first two approximations hold under the uniform distribution over $u\in \F_q^m$,
   439		whereas there is no question distribution associated with the third approximation.
   440	\end{theorem}
   441	
   442	\begin{proof}
   443	Let $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$
   444	where $m, d, \ldc \in \N$ are integers, $q \in \N$ is an admissible field size,
   445	and $m$ divides $q$. Let $\Sigma=\F_q$. Let $\code \subseteq \Sigma^q$ be the Reed-Solomon code with degree $d$. Explicitly, $\code$ is the set of all $(p(x_1),\ldots,p(x_n))$ where $p:\F_q\to\F_q$ is a univariate polynomial of degree at most $d$ and $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ are an enumeration of $\F_q$. Then in the (standard) notation from~\cite{ji2021quantum} $\code$ is a linear $[q,d+1,n-d+1]_\Sigma$ code.
   446	
   447	Observe that the two-prover tensor code test, for the code $\code^{\otimes m}$, as described in~\cite[Figure 1 and Figure 2]{ji2021quantum}, is identical to the game $\game^\ld$ with parameters $\ldparams$ and $\ldc=1$, whose decider is presented in Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider}. This is because 
   448	\begin{enumerate}
   449	\item The \emph{axis-parallel line-versus-point test} from Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider} is identical to the \emph{axis-parallel lines test} from~\cite[Figure 1]{ji2021quantum}, with the only difference that in Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider} the roles of A and B are chosen uniformly at random. This is consistent with the two-prover variant of the tensor code test from~\cite[Section 4.1]{ji2021quantum}.
   450	\item The \emph{diagonal line-versus-point test} from Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider} is identical to the \emph{subcube commutation test} from~\cite[Figure 1]{ji2021quantum}, with again the added symmetrization between players. 
   451	\item The \emph{consistency test} from Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider} is identical to the \emph{synchronicity test} from~\cite[Figure 2]{ji2021quantum}.
   452	\end{enumerate}
   453	
   454	As a result,~\cite[Theorem 4.7]{ji2021quantum}, in which we choose the parameter $k$ as $k=m^3d$,  immediately yields \Cref{lem:ld-soundness}.
   455	
   456	To conclude it remains to extend the result to the case of general $\ldc$. This is done 
   457	via a standard reduction, following exactly the same steps as the derivation of Theorem 4.43 from Theorem 4.40 in~\cite{NW19}.
   458	\end{proof}

   465	\subsubsection{Complexity of the classical low-degree test.}
   466	The CL functions and decision procedure of the low-degree test are incorporated
   467	as subroutines in some of the normal form verifiers constructed in subsequent
   468	sections.
   469	The next lemma establishes the time complexity of these procedures as a function
   470	of the parameter tuple $\ldparams = (q,m,d,k)$.
   471	The lemma also establishes the time complexity of computing the {description} of
   472	the decision procedure $\decider^\ld$ as a Turing machine, given the parameter
   473	tuple $\ldparams$ as input.
   474	
   475	
   476	
   477	\begin{lemma}[Complexity of the classical low-degree test]
   478	  \label{lem:ld-complexity}
   479	  Let $\ldparams = (q,m,d,k)$ denote a parameter tuple.
   480	  \begin{enumerate}
   481		\item The time complexity of the decision procedure $\decider^\ld$
   482	    parametrized by $\ldparams$ is $\poly(m, d, k, \log q)$.
   483		\item The time complexity of evaluating marginals of the CL functions
   484	    $L_\Point$, $L_\ALine$, and $L_\DLine$ at a given input point is $\poly(m, \log
   485	    q)$.
   486		\item The Turing machine description of the decision procedure $\decider^\ld$
   487	    parametrized by $\ldparams$ can be computed from $\ldparams$ in $\polylog
   488	    (q,m,d,k)$ time.
   489	  \end{enumerate}
   490	\end{lemma}
   491	
   492	\begin{proof}

  1232	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:pauli-completeness}

  1236	\begin{proof}
  1237	  We begin by specifying the value-$1$ strategy $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, E)$.
  1238	  The state is
  1239	  \begin{equation*}
  1240	    \ket{\psi} = \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M} \otimes \ket{\EPR_2}\;.
  1241	  \end{equation*}

  1243	  We start with measurements associated with questions of type $\Point$,
  1244	  $\ALine$, $\DLine$, and $\Pauli$.
  1245	  Using notation introduced in Section~\ref{sec:ld-encoding}, for $W \in \{X,
  1246	  Z\}$,
  1247	  \begin{align*}
  1248	    E^{(\Point,W),\, y}_{\, a}
  1249	    & = \tau^W_{[g_{\cdot}(y) = a]} \otimes I\;,\\
  1250	    E^{(\ALine,W),\, \line}_{\, f}
  1251	    & = \tau^W_{[(g_{\cdot})|_\line = f]} \otimes I\;,\\
  1252	    E^{(\DLine,W),\, \line}_{\, f}
  1253	    & = \tau^W_{[(g_{\cdot})|_\line = f]} \otimes I\;,\\    
  1254	    E^{(\Pauli,W)}_{\, a}
  1255	    & = \tau^W_{a} \otimes I\;.
  1256	  \end{align*}
  1257	  Here, the bracket notation used to post-process measurement outcomes is
  1258	  defined in \Cref{def:bracket}.
  1259	  Thus, for example, the measurement on question $((\Point,W),y)$ corresponds to
  1260	  first performing the measurement $\{\tau^W_h\}_{h \in \F_q^M}$, receiving an
  1261	  outcome $h \in \F_q^M$, and then outputting the value $a = g_{h}(y)$.
  1262	
  1263	  For $\ALine$ and $\DLine$ questions, the question content $\line$ denotes
  1264	  either an axis-parallel line $\line(u_0,e_i)$ for some $i \in
  1265	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$, or a diagonal line $\line(u_0,v')$ for some $v' \in
  1266	  \F_q^m$.
  1267	  As described at the beginning of \Cref{sec:qld-game}, axis-parallel lines are
  1268	  specified by pairs $(u_0,s) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q$ and diagonal lines are
  1269	  specified by triples $(u_0,s,v) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q \times \F_q^m$.
  1270	  The measurement on question $((\ALine,W),\line)$, for example, corresponds to
  1271	  first performing the measurement $\{\tau^W_h\}_{h \in \F_q^M}$ to get an
  1272	  outcome $h \in \F_q^M$, and reporting the univariate polynomial $f_\line(t) =
  1273	  g_{h}(u_0 + te_i)$ where $\line$ is specified by $(u_0,s)$ and $i = \chi(s)$.
  1274	  
  1275	
  1276	
  1277	  Next we specify the POVMs associated with questions of type $\Constraint$,
  1278	  $\Variable$, and $\Pair$.
  1279	  Questions with these question types have a question content that is a tuple
  1280	  $\omega= (u_\xpt, u_\zpt, r_\xpt, r_\zpt)\in (\F_q^m)^2 \times \F_q^2$.
  1281	  Given such a tuple, consider the two $\F_2$-valued POVMs $A=\{A_b\}_{b \in
  1282	    \F_2}$ and $B=\{B_b\}_{b \in \F_2}$ defined as
  1283	  \begin{align}
  1284	    A_b & = \tau^X_{[\tr(g_{\cdot}(u_X)\, r_\xpt) = b]} \otimes I\;,\label{eq:gonna-expand-A}\\
  1285	    B_b & = \tau^Z_{[\tr(g_{\cdot}(u_Z)\, r_\zpt) = b]} \otimes I\;.\label{eq:gonna-expand-B}
  1286	  \end{align}
  1287	  We would like to determine when the two observables $\mathcal{O}_A = A_0 -
  1288	  A_1$ and $\mathcal{O}_B = B_0 - B_1$ commute or anti-commute.
  1289	  Towards this we derive alternative expressions for these observables from
  1290	  which their commutativity becomes plain from inspection.
  1291	  We begin by inspecting the first matrices on the right-hand sides of
  1292	  Equations~\eqref{eq:gonna-expand-A} and~\eqref{eq:gonna-expand-B}:
  1293	  \begin{align}
  1294	  \tau^W_{[\tr(g_{\cdot}(u_W)\, r_W) = b]}
  1295	  &= \sum_{h : \tr(g_{h}(u_W)\, r_W) = b} \tau^W_h\nonumber\\
  1296	  &= \sum_{h : \tr((h\, \cdot\, \ind_{m}(u_W)) \cdot r_W ) = b} \tau^W_h\;,\label{eq:expand-with-dot-product}
  1297	  \end{align}
  1298	  where~\eqref{eq:expand-with-dot-product}
  1299	  follows by  Definition~\ref{eq:low-degree-encoding-definition}.
  1300	  As a result,
  1301	  \begin{align}
  1302	&  \tau^W_{[\tr(g_{\cdot}(u_W)\, r_W) = 0]}
  1303	  -   \tau^W_{[\tr(g_{\cdot}(u_W)\, r_W) = 1]} \notag \\
  1304	  & = \sum_{h : \tr((h\, \cdot\, \ind_{m}(u_W)) \cdot r_W ) = 0} \tau^W_h
  1305	  	- \sum_{h : \tr((h\, \cdot\, \ind_{m}(u_W)) \cdot r_W ) = 1} \tau^W_h\nonumber\\
  1306	  & = \sum_{h} (-1)^{\tr((h\, \cdot\, \ind_{m}(u_W)) \cdot r_W )} \tau^W_h\nonumber\\
  1307	  & = \tau^W(\ind_{m}(u_W)r_W)\;,\label{eq:finally-got-an-observable}
  1308	  \end{align}
  1309	  where the last step uses~\eqref{eq:pauli-obs-proj}.
  1310	  As a result, Equation~\eqref{eq:finally-got-an-observable}
  1311	  and Equations~\eqref{eq:gonna-expand-A} and~\eqref{eq:gonna-expand-B} imply that
  1312	  \begin{equation*}
  1313	  \mathcal{O}_A = \tau^X(\ind_{m}(u_X)r_X) \otimes I,\quad
  1314	  \mathcal{O}_B = \tau^Z(\ind_{m}(u_Z)r_Z) \otimes I\;.
  1315	  \end{equation*}
  1316	  Now, let $\gamma = \tr((\ind_{m}(u_X)r_X) \cdot (\ind_{m}(u_Z)r_Z)) \in \F_2$,
  1317	  as in Equation~\eqref{eq:gamma-value}.

  1319	  \begin{equation*}
  1320	  \mathcal{O}_A \mathcal{O}_B = (-1)^{\gamma} \mathcal{O}_B \mathcal{O}_A\;.
  1321	  \end{equation*}
  1322	  As a result, $\gamma$ quantifies whether the observables $\mathcal{O}_A$ and
  1323	  $\mathcal{O}_B$ commute, and therefore whether the measurements~$A$ and~$B$
  1324	  commute.
  1325	  If $\gamma = 0$, they commute.
  1326	  If $\gamma = 1$, they anti-commute.
  1327	  We now specify the POVMs associated with questions of type $\Constraint$,
  1328	  $\Variable$, and $\Pair$, considering separately the cases when $\gamma = 0$
  1329	  or $\gamma = 1$.
  1330	  \begin{enumerate}
  1331	  \item If $\gamma = 0$, 
  1332	     for each $\beta_X, \beta_Z \in \F_2$ define
  1333	    \begin{equation}\label{eq:pair-definition}
  1334	      E^{\Pair,\, \omega}_{\beta_X,\, \beta_Z} = A_{\beta_X} \cdot B_{\beta_Z}\;,
  1335	    \end{equation}
  1336	    \begin{equation*}
  1337	      E^{(\Pair,X),\, \omega}_{a} = A_{a} \;,\qquad
  1338	      E^{(\Pair,Z),\, \omega}_{a} = B_{a}\;.
  1339	    \end{equation*}
  1340	    The POVM associated with questions of type $\Constraint$ and $\Variable$ are
  1341	    defined to be trivial.
  1342	    In particular, we define
  1343	    \begin{equation*}
  1344	      E^{\Constraint_i,\, \omega}_{\, 0,\, 0,\, 0}
  1345	      = E^{\Variable_j,\, \omega}_{\, 0} = I\;,
  1346	    \end{equation*}
  1347	    and the remaining POVM elements in these measurements are set to be zero.
  1348	  \item If $\gamma = 1$, then $\mathcal{O}_A$ and $\mathcal{O}_B$ anti-commute.
  1349	    In this case we define measurements $E^{\Constraint_i,\, \omega}$ and
  1350	    $E^{\Variable_j,\, \omega}$, for all $i\in\{1,\ldots,6\}$ and $j
  1351	    \in\{1,\ldots,9\}$ to be those guaranteed by Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}.
  1352	    Measurements associated with inputs of type $\Pair$ are defined to be
  1353	    trivial.
  1354	    In particular, we define
  1355	    \begin{equation*}
  1356	      E^{\Pair,\, \omega}_{0,\, 0} = E^{(\Pair,X),\, \omega}_{0} = E^{(\Pair,Z),\, \omega}_{0} = I\;,
  1357	    \end{equation*}
  1358	    and the remaining matrices in these measurements are set to be zero.
  1359	  \end{enumerate}
  1360	  This completes the specification of the strategy.
  1361	
  1362	  Now, we show that $\strategy$ is a value-$1$ SPCC strategy.
  1363	  It is clearly symmetric and projective. 
  1364	  To show that it is consistent, we note that all measurements are Pauli basis
  1365	  measurements, which are consistent, or measurements produced by
  1366	  Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}, which are also consistent.

  1387		Consider first the first three tests executed by the decision procedure in

  1426	\paragraph{Soundness of the Pauli basis test.} 
  1427	We state the soundness properties of the Pauli basis test.
  1428	The following is an adaptation of the self-testing statement in~\cite[Theorem
  1429	6.4]{NW19}.
  1430	
  1431	\begin{theorem}
  1432	  \label{thm:pauli}
  1433	There exists a function 
  1434	\[\delta_{\qld}(\eps,m,d,q) = a(md)^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})\]
  1435	 for universal constants $a \geq 1$ and $0 < b < 1$ such that the following holds. For all admissible parameter tuples $\qldparams = (q,m,d)$ and for all strategies $\strategy = (\ket{\psi},A,B)$ for the game $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ that succeed with probability at least $1 - \eps$, there exist local isometries $\phi_\alice: \mH_\alice \to \mH_{\alice'} \otimes \mH_{\alice''},\phi_\bob: \mH_\bob \to \mH_{\bob'} \otimes \mH_{\bob''}$ (where $\ket{\psi} \in \mH_\alice \otimes \mH_\bob$ and $\mH_{\alice''},\mH_{\bob''} \cong (\C^q)^{\otimes M}$ with $M = 2^m$) and a state $\ket{\aux} \in \mH_{\alice'} \otimes \mH_{\bob'}$ such that 
  1436	\begin{enumerate}
  1437	    \item $\left \| \phi_\alice \otimes \phi_B \ket{\psi} - \ket{\aux} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}  \right \| \leq \delta_{\qld}(\eps,m,d,q)$,
  1438	    \item Letting $\tilde{A}^x_a = \phi_A\, A^x_a \, \phi_A^\dagger$ and $\tilde{B}^y_b = \phi_B B^y_b \phi_B^\dagger$, we have for $W \in \{X,Z\}$
  1439	    \begin{gather*}
  1440	        \tilde{A}^{(\pauli,W)}_u \otimes I_{\bob'\bob''} \approx_{\delta_{\qld}} (\tau^W_u)_{\alice''} \otimes I_{\alice' \bob' \bob''} \\
  1441	        I_{\alice'\alice''} \otimes \tilde{B}^{(\pauli,W)}_u    \approx_{\delta_{\qld}} I_{\alice' \alice'' \bob'} \otimes (\tau^W_u)_{\bob''}\;,
  1442	    \end{gather*}
  1443	    where the $\approx_{\delta_{\qld}}$ statement holds with respect to the state $\ket{\aux}_{\alice'\bob'} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}_{\alice''\bob''}$ and the answer summation is over $u \in \F_q^M$.
  1444	\end{enumerate}
  1445	\end{theorem}

  1447	We provide a proof of \Cref{thm:pauli} in \Cref{sec:qld-analysis}.

  1451	However, it is more convenient for our application of the Pauli basis test to
  1452	instead deal with \emph{qubits}.
  1453	In particular, we use the Pauli basis test in the ``introspection game'' of
  1454	Section~\ref{sec:introspection}, where the players are commanded to sample

  1456	By definition of normal form verifier, $\sampler$ is a sampler over $\F_2$, and
  1457	therefore it is natural to use a test for qubit Pauli measurements.

  1460	shows that the conclusions of \Cref{thm:pauli} can also be described in terms of
  1461	testing for maximally entangled states over qubits and qubit Pauli measurements.

  1492	\subsubsection{Canonical parameters and complexity of the Pauli basis test}
  1493	\label{sec:qld-complexity}
  1494	
  1495	We specify a canonical setting of the parameter tuple $\qldparams$ as a function
  1496	of an integer $R$.
  1497	We call this canonical setting $\introparams$ because we use these in the
  1498	``introspection'' section (\Cref{sec:introspection}).
  1499	We then give bounds on the complexity of computing the decision procedure and CL
  1500	functions of the Pauli basis test corresponding to the parameter tuple
  1501	$\qldparams$, as a function of $R$.
  1502	
  1503	\begin{definition}[Canonical parameters of the Pauli basis test]
  1504	  \label{def:introparams}
  1505	  Let $a,b$ be the universal constants specified in Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli}.
  1506	  Let $c$ denote the smallest even integer that is at least $(b + a)/b$.
  1507	  For all integers $R \geq 4$, define the tuple $\introparams(R) = (q,m,d)$
  1508	  where
  1509	  \begin{itemize}
  1510	  	\item $q = 2^k$ for $k = c \lceil  \log \log R  \rceil + 1$.
  1511		\item $m = 2^j$ where $2^j \leq c \lceil \log R \rceil + 1 < 2^{j+1}$. 
  1512		\item $d = 1$. 
  1513	  \end{itemize}
  1514	\end{definition}
  1515	
  1516	Intuitively, this choice of parameters is such that the Pauli basis test
  1517	certifies the presence of an $M=2^m$-qudit EPR state (of local dimension $q$), or
  1518	equivalently an $M\log q$-qubit EPR state.
  1519	
  1520	\begin{lemma}
  1521	  \label{lem:delta-bound}
  1522	 For all integers $R \geq 4$, the parameter tuple $\introparams(R) = (q,m,d)$ is
  1523	  admissible (see Definition~\ref{def:admissible}), satisfies $2^m \geq R$, and furthermore there exist
  1524	  universal constants $a'\geq 1$ and $0 < b' \leq 1$ such that the function
  1525	  $\delta_\qld(\eps, m, d, q)$ from Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli} is at most
  1526	   \[
  1527	   	a' ( \log(R)^{a'} \cdot \eps^{b'} + \log(R)^{-b'}) \;.
  1528		\]
  1529	\end{lemma}
  1530	
  1531	\begin{proof}
  1532	  We verify the admissibility of $\introparams(R)$ first: the field size $q =
  1533	  2^k$ is admissible because $k$ is odd. We have $m | q$ because for all $R \geq 4$ we have  
  1534	  \[
  1535	  	2^j \leq 2 c \lceil \log R \rceil \leq 2 \log^c R \leq 2^k~.
  1536	  \]
  1537		Next, we show that $R \leq 2^m$. Since $m = 2^j \geq (c/2) \log R$, we have that
  1538		\[

  1540		\]

  1542	
  1543	Finally, we show the desired bound on the error function $\delta_\qld(\eps,m,d,q)$. First, observe that $2^{-bmd} \leq q^{-b}$ because $k \leq m$.
  1544	  Note that for $R \geq 2$, we have $m \leq 2c \log R$, and furthermore $q =
  1545	  2^k \geq \log^c R$.
  1546	Then, we get
  1547	\begin{align*}
  1548	  	\delta_\qld(\eps,m,d,q)
  1549	    & = a (md)^a (\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd}) \tag{by Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli}}  \\
  1550	    & \leq a (md)^a (\eps^b + 2q^{-b}) \tag{because  $2^{-bmd} \leq q^{-b}$}  \\
  1551	    & = a (m)^a (\eps^b + 2q^{-b}) \tag{because  $d=1$}  \\
  1552	    & \leq a (2c)^a \log^{a} (R) ( \eps^{b} + 2q^{-b}) \tag{because  $m \leq 2c \log R$}\\
  1553	    & \leq a (2c)^a \log^{a} (R) ( \eps^{b} + 2(\log R)^{-cb}) \tag{because  $q \geq \log^c R$}\\
  1554	    & \leq 2a (2c)^a \log^{a} (R) ( \eps^{b} + (\log R)^{-cb}) \\
  1555	    & = 2a (2c)^a ( (\log R)^{a}\eps^{b} + (\log R)^{a-cb}) \\
  1556	    & \leq 2a(2c)^{a} \left ( (\log R)^{a} \eps^{b}
  1557	      + (\log R)^{-b} \right) \tag{because  $cb - a \geq b \geq 0$}\\

  1559	  \end{align*}
  1560	  where $a'$ is defined as the quantity $2a(2c)^a$.
  1561	This completes the proof of the lemma.
  1562	\end{proof}

   182	level-3 assertion in `def:ld-question-distribution`, blueprint

   190	/-- The question alphabet for the low-degree game (`def:ld-game`, blueprint
   191	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-31`; paper origin

   193	-/

   203	    (uniformDistribution ((LdType × LdType) × LdSpace P))
   204	    (fun s =>

   207	/-- The coefficient-tuple answer alphabet of the low-degree game.  Polynomial
   208	answers are representatives with exactly the coefficient lengths printed in
   209	the paper, as required by `def:ld-win-predicate` (blueprint
   210	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:56-105`; paper
   211	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`).

   214	  | pointVals (a : Fin P.k → ScalarQ P)
   215	  | alinePolys (a : Fin P.k → Fin (P.d + 1) → ScalarQ P)
   216	  | dlinePolys (a : Fin P.k → Fin (P.m * P.d + 1) → ScalarQ P)
   217	  deriving DecidableEq

   219	/-- A finite sum code used only to provide the answer alphabet's `Fintype`
   220	instance; the public constructors are those of `def:ld-win-predicate`,

   222	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
   223	-/
   224	abbrev LdAnswerCode (P : LdParams) :=
   225	  (Fin P.k → ScalarQ P) ⊕
   226	    ((Fin P.k → Fin (P.d + 1) → ScalarQ P) ⊕
   227	      (Fin P.k → Fin (P.m * P.d + 1) → ScalarQ P))

   230	finite-carrier infrastructure for `def:ld-win-predicate`, blueprint
   231	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:56-105`, paper origin
   232	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`).

   234	noncomputable def ldAnswerEquiv (P : LdParams) :

   236	  toFun
   237	    | .pointVals a => .inl a
   238	    | .alinePolys a => .inr (.inl a)
   239	    | .dlinePolys a => .inr (.inr a)

   241	    | .inl a => .pointVals a
   242	    | .inr (.inl a) => .alinePolys a
   243	    | .inr (.inr a) => .dlinePolys a
   244	  left_inv := by intro x; cases x <;> rfl
   245	  right_inv := by
   246	    intro x
   247	    cases x with
   248	    | inl a => rfl
   249	    | inr x =>
   250	        cases x with
   251	        | inl a => rfl
   252	        | inr a => rfl

   254	instance (P : LdParams) : Inhabited (LdAnswer P) :=

   256	
   257	noncomputable instance (P : LdParams) : Fintype (LdAnswer P) :=
   258	  Fintype.ofEquiv (LdAnswerCode P) (ldAnswerEquiv P).symm
   259	
   260	/-- Evaluation of a coefficient tuple at a field element.  This is the
   261	representative convention used by the line answers in `def:ld-win-predicate`,
   262	blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:56-105`, paper origin
   263	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
   264	-/
   265	def evalCoefficient {K : Type*} [Semiring K] {n : ℕ}
   266	    (c : Fin n → K) (t : K) : K :=
   267	  ∑ i : Fin n, c i * t ^ i.val
   268	
   269	/-- Check that an answer has the constructor prescribed by its question type;
   270	Lean encoding of the rejection clause in `def:ld-win-predicate`, blueprint
   271	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:56-105`, paper origin
   272	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
   273	-/
   274	def validLdAnswer {P : LdParams} (t : LdType) (a : LdAnswer P) : Bool :=
   275	  match t, a with
   276	  | .point, .pointVals _ => true
   277	  | .aline, .alinePolys _ => true
   278	  | .dline, .dlinePolys _ => true
   279	  | _, _ => false
   280	
   281	/-- The axis-parallel line/point relation in `def:ld-win-predicate`, blueprint
   282	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:56-105`, paper origin
   283	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
   284	-/
   285	def alinePointCondition (P : LdParams) (line point : LdSpace P)
   286	    (f : Fin P.k → Fin (P.d + 1) → ScalarQ P)
   287	    (a : Fin P.k → ScalarQ P) : Prop :=
   288	  -- Universal quantification follows the zero-direction convention in
   289	  -- `rem:ld-win-zero-direction`.
   290	  ∀ t : ScalarQ P,
   291	    point.point = line.point + t • coordinateDirection (chiIndex P line.seed) →
   292	      ∀ j : Fin P.k, evalCoefficient (f j) t = a j
   293	
   294	/-- The diagonal line/point relation in `def:ld-win-predicate`, blueprint
   295	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:56-105`, paper origin
   296	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
   297	-/
   298	def dlinePointCondition (P : LdParams) (line point : LdSpace P)
   299	    (f : Fin P.k → Fin (P.m * P.d + 1) → ScalarQ P)
   300	    (a : Fin P.k → ScalarQ P) : Prop :=
   301	  ∀ t : ScalarQ P,
   302	    point.point = line.point + t • line.direction →
   303	      ∀ j : Fin P.k, evalCoefficient (f j) t = a j
   304	
   305	/-- The low-degree consistency predicate, rejecting answers of the wrong
   306	constructor shape.  This is `def:ld-win-predicate` in
   307	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:56-105`, paper origin
   308	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
   309	-/
   310	noncomputable def ldWinPredicate (P : LdParams) :
   311	    LdQuestion P → LdQuestion P → LdAnswer P → LdAnswer P → Bool :=
   312	  open Classical in
   313	  fun (tA, xA) (tB, xB) a b =>

   318	            decide (alinePointCondition P xA xB f u)
   319	        | .point, .aline, .pointVals u, .alinePolys f =>
   320	            decide (alinePointCondition P xB xA f u)

    26	polynomials. This is Mathlib's `MvPolynomial.restrictDegree` submodule. -/
    27	noncomputable abbrev polyFunc (m : ℕ) (K : Type*) [CommSemiring K] (d : ℕ) :
    28	    Submodule K (MvPolynomial (Fin m) K) :=
    29	  MvPolynomial.restrictDegree (Fin m) K d

    31	/-- If `p ∈ polyFunc m K d`, then `p.degreeOf i ≤ d` for every variable `i`. -/
    32	theorem degreeOf_le_of_mem_polyFunc {m d : ℕ} {K : Type*} [CommSemiring K]
    33	    {p : MvPolynomial (Fin m) K} (hp : p ∈ polyFunc m K d) (i : Fin m) :
    34	    p.degreeOf i ≤ d :=
    35	  MvPolynomial.degreeOf_le_iff.mpr fun s hs =>
    36	    (MvPolynomial.mem_restrictDegree (σ := Fin m) (R := K) p d).mp hp s hs i

    42	theorem polyFuncMonotone {m d : ℕ} {K : Type*} [CommSemiring K] :

    44	  intro p hp
    45	  rw [MvPolynomial.mem_restrictDegree] at hp ⊢
    46	  intro s hs i
    47	  exact (hp s hs i).trans (Nat.le_succ d)

    49	/-- The uniform agreement probability of two polynomials on `K^m`, written as a
    50	finite cardinality ratio over `K^m`. -/
    51	noncomputable def polynomialAgreementProbability (m : ℕ) (K : Type*) [Field K] [Fintype K]
    52	    [DecidableEq K] (g h : MvPolynomial (Fin m) K) : ℚ≥0 :=
    53	  #{x ∈ (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin m → K)) |
    54	      MvPolynomial.eval x g = MvPolynomial.eval x h} /
    55	    (Fintype.card K ^ m : ℚ≥0)

    57	/-- If every individual degree of `p` is at most `d`, then the total degree of
    58	`p` is at most `m * d`. -/
    59	theorem totalDegree_le_mul_of_degreeOf_le {m d : ℕ} {K : Type*} [CommSemiring K]
    60	    {p : MvPolynomial (Fin m) K} (hdeg : ∀ i, p.degreeOf i ≤ d) :
    61	    p.totalDegree ≤ m * d := by
    62	  rw [MvPolynomial.totalDegree]
    63	  refine Finset.sup_le ?_
    64	  intro s hs
    65	  calc
    66	    s.sum (fun _ e => e) = ∑ i : Fin m, s i := by
    67	      rw [Finsupp.sum_fintype]
    68	      intro i
    69	      rfl
    70	    _ ≤ ∑ _i : Fin m, d := by
    71	      refine Finset.sum_le_sum ?_
    72	      intro i _
    73	      exact (MvPolynomial.degreeOf_le_iff.mp (hdeg i)) s hs
    74	    _ = m * d := by
    75	      simp [Fintype.card_fin]

    77	/-- If two polynomials on `K^m` have total degree at most `d`, then the uniform
    78	agreement probability is at most `d / |K|`. -/
    79	theorem schwartzZippel_totalDegree {m d : ℕ} {K : Type*} [Field K] [Fintype K]
    80	    [DecidableEq K] {g h : MvPolynomial (Fin m) K} (hneq : g ≠ h)
    81	    (hg : g.totalDegree ≤ d) (hh : h.totalDegree ≤ d) :
    82	    polynomialAgreementProbability m K g h ≤ d / Fintype.card K := by
    83	  have hsub_ne : g - h ≠ 0 := sub_ne_zero.mpr hneq
    84	  have hsub_deg : (g - h).totalDegree ≤ d :=
    85	    (MvPolynomial.totalDegree_sub g h).trans (max_le hg hh)
    86	  unfold polynomialAgreementProbability
    87	  rw [show {x ∈ (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin m → K)) |
    88	        MvPolynomial.eval x g = MvPolynomial.eval x h} =
    89	      {x ∈ (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin m → K)) |
    90	        MvPolynomial.eval x (g - h) = 0} by
    91	        ext x
    92	        simp [MvPolynomial.eval_sub, sub_eq_zero]]
    93	  calc
    94	    #{x ∈ (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin m → K)) |
    95	        MvPolynomial.eval x (g - h) = 0} /
    96	        (Fintype.card K ^ m : ℚ≥0)
    97	      ≤ (g - h).totalDegree / Fintype.card K := by
    98	          simpa using
    99	            (MvPolynomial.schwartz_zippel_totalDegree
   100	              (n := m) (p := g - h) hsub_ne (Finset.univ : Finset K))
   101	    _ ≤ d / Fintype.card K := by
   102	          gcongr

   104	/-- Schwartz-Zippel for the paper's low-individual-degree class
   105	`\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}`. -/
   106	theorem schwartzZippel_individualDegree {m d : ℕ} {K : Type*} [Field K] [Fintype K]
   107	    [DecidableEq K] (g h : polyFunc m K d) (hneq : g ≠ h) :
   108	    polynomialAgreementProbability m K g.1 h.1 ≤ ((m * d : ℕ) : ℚ≥0) / Fintype.card K := by
   109	  have hval_ne : g.1 ≠ h.1 := by
   110	    intro hgh
   111	    apply hneq
   112	    exact Subtype.ext hgh
   113	  have hg_degOf : ∀ i, g.1.degreeOf i ≤ d :=
   114	    degreeOf_le_of_mem_polyFunc g.property
   115	  have hh_degOf : ∀ i, h.1.degreeOf i ≤ d :=
   116	    degreeOf_le_of_mem_polyFunc h.property
   117	  exact schwartzZippel_totalDegree (g := g.1) (h := h.1) hval_ne
   118	    (totalDegree_le_mul_of_degreeOf_le hg_degOf)
   119	    (totalDegree_le_mul_of_degreeOf_le hh_degOf)

   512	\subsection{The Magic Square game}
   513	\label{sec:ms}
   514	
   515	We recall the \emph{Magic Square game} of Mermin and
   516	Peres~\cite{mermin1990simple,peres1990incompatible,aravind2002simple}.
   517	The Magic Square game is a simple self-test for EPR pairs (it tests for two of
   518	them). In addition, it allows one to test that a pair of observables
   519	\emph{anticommutes}.
   520	Here we use it as a building block to construct the quantum low-degree test. 
   521	
   522	There are several formulations of the Magic Square game; here we present it as a
   523	\emph{binary constraint satisfaction} game~\cite{cleve2014characterization}.
   524	In this formulation of the game (denoted by $\game_\MS$) there are $6$ linear
   525	equations defined over $9$ variables that take values in $\F_2$.
   526	The variables correspond to the cells of a $3 \times 3$ grid, as depicted in
   527	Figure~\ref{fig:ms}.
   528	Five of the equations correspond to the constraint that the sum of the variables
   529	in each row and the first two columns must be equal to $0$, and the last
   530	equation requires that the sum of the variables in the last column must be equal
   531	to $1$.
   532	
   533	\begin{figure}[ht!]
   534		\begin{center}
   535	    \renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.6}
   536			\begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|}
   537				\hline
   538				$x_1$ & $x_2$ & $x_3$ \\
   539				\hline 
   540				$x_4$ & $x_5$ & $x_6$ \\	
   541				\hline
   542				$x_7$ & $x_8$ & $x_9$ \\
   543				\hline
   544			\end{tabular}
   545			\caption{The Magic Square game}
   546			\label{fig:ms}
   547			\end{center}
   548	\end{figure}
   549	
   550	The question set $\type^\ms$ of the Magic Square game is the following:
   551	\begin{equation*}
   552	  \begin{split}
   553	    \type^\msc & = \{ \Constraint_i : i = 1, 2, \ldots, 6\}\;,\\
   554	    \type^\msv & = \{ \Variable_j : j = 1, 2, \ldots, 9\}\;,\\
   555	    \type^\ms & = \type^\msc \cup \type^\msv\;.
   556	  \end{split}
   557	\end{equation*}
   558	The questions $\Constraint_i$ for $i \in \{1,2,3\}$ correspond to the three row
   559	constraints, the questions $\Constraint_4$, $\Constraint_5$ correspond to the first
   560	two column constraints, and question $\Constraint_6$ corresponds to the third
   561	column constraint.
   562	
   563	In the Magic Square game, the verifier first samples a constraint $\Constraint_i
   564	\in \type^\msc$ uniformly at random, and then samples $\Variable_j$, one of the
   565	three variables in the row or column corresponding to $\Constraint_i$, uniformly
   566	at random.
   567	One player is randomly assigned to be the $\Constraint$ player, and the other is
   568	assigned to be the $\Variable$ player.
   569	The $\Constraint$ player is sent the question $\Constraint_i$ and is expected to
   570	respond with three bits $(\beta_{v_1}, \beta_{v_2}, \beta_{v_3}) \in \F_2^3$,
   571	where $(v_1,v_2,v_3)$ are the indices of the three variables corresponding to
   572	$\Constraint_i$.
   573	The $\Variable$ player is given question $\Variable_j$ and is expected to
   574	respond with a single bit $\gamma \in \F_2$.
   575	The players win if the $\Constraint$ player's answers satisfy the equation
   576	associated with $\Constraint_i$, and $\gamma = \beta_j$.
   577	More precisely, the verifier samples an edge of the type graph (see Section~\ref{sec:types}) $G^\ms$
   578	in Fig.~\ref{fig:type-graph-ms}, sends one endpoint to a random player, and the
   579	other endpoint to the other player.

   612	The following theorem records the self-testing (also known as \emph{rigidity})
   613	properties of the Magic Square game.
   614	Its self-testing properties
   615	are crucial to the Pauli basis test.
   616	In particular, it is used to enforce anticommutation relations between certain
   617	pairs of operators.
   618	We will refer to this theorem in the proof of the soundness of the Pauli basis test (\Cref{thm:pauli} below) in \Cref{sec:qld-analysis}.
   619	
   620	\begin{theorem}[Rigidity of the Magic Square game]
   621	  \label{thm:ms-rigidity}
   622	
   623	
   624	Let $\strategy = (\ket{\psi},A,B)$ be a strategy that succeeds in the Magic Square game $\game^{\MS}$ with probability $1 - \eps$, where $\ket{\psi} \in \mH_A \otimes \mH_B$ is a state. Then there exist local isometries $\phi_A: \mH_A \to \mH_{A'} \otimes \mH_{A''},\phi_B: \mH_B \to \mH_{B'} \otimes \mH_{B''}$ (where $\mH_{A'},\mH_{B'} \cong (\C^2)^{\otimes 2}$ and $\mH_{A''},\mH_{B''}$ are finite dimensional) and a state $\ket{\aux} \in \mH_{A''} \otimes \mH_{B''}$ such that 
   625	\begin{enumerate}
   626	    \item $\left \| \phi_A \otimes \phi_B \ket{\psi} - \ket{\EPR_2}^{\otimes 2} \otimes \ket{\aux} \right \| \leq O(\sqrt{\eps})$,
   627	    \item Letting $\tilde{A}^x_a = \phi_A\, A^x_a \, \phi_A^\dagger$ and $\tilde{B}^y_b = \phi_B B^y_b \phi_B^\dagger$, we have that
   628	    \begin{gather*}
   629	        \tilde{A}^{\Variable_1}_b \otimes I_{B'B''} \approx_{\sqrt{\eps}} (\sigma^X_b)_{A'} \otimes I_{A'' B' B''} \\
   630	        \tilde{A}^{\Variable_5}_b \otimes I_{B'B''} \approx_{\sqrt{\eps}} (\sigma^Z_b)_{A'} \otimes I_{A'' B' B''} \\
   631	        I_{A'A''} \otimes \tilde{B}^{\Variable_1}_b    \approx_{\sqrt{\eps}} I_{A' A'' B''} \otimes (\sigma^X_b)_{B'} \\
   632	        I_{A'A''} \otimes \tilde{B}^{\Variable_5}_b    \approx_{\sqrt{\eps}} I_{A' A'' B''} \otimes (\sigma^Z_b)_{B'}
   633	    \end{gather*}
   634	    where the $\approx_{\sqrt{\eps}}$ statement holds with respect to the state $\ket{\EPR_2}^{\otimes 2}_{A'B'} \otimes \ket{\aux}_{A''B''}$ and the answer summation is over $b \in \{0,1\}$. As a consequence, letting 
   635	    \begin{gather*}
   636	    \tilde{A}^{\Variable_1} = \tilde{A}^{\Variable_1}_0 - \tilde{A}^{\Variable_1}_1 \\
   637	    \tilde{A}^{\Variable_5} = \tilde{A}^{\Variable_5}_0 - \tilde{A}^{\Variable_5}_1 \\
   638	    \end{gather*}
   639	    it holds that
   640	    \begin{gather*}
   641	        \tilde{A}^{\Variable_1} \tilde{A}^{\Variable_5} \otimes I_{B' B''} \approx_{\sqrt{\eps}} - \tilde{A}^{\Variable_5}  \tilde{A}^{\Variable_1} \otimes I_{B' B''} \\
   642	        I_{A' A''} \otimes \tilde{B}^{\Variable_1} \tilde{B}^{\Variable_5}  \approx_{\sqrt{\eps}} - I_{A' A''} \otimes \tilde{B}^{\Variable_5}  \tilde{B}^{\Variable_1} \;,
   643	      \end{gather*}
   644	      where the notation $M \approx_{\delta} N$ for $M, N$ that are not POVM
   645	      elements means
   646	      \[  \bra{\psi} (M-N)^\dagger (M-N) \ket{\psi}  \leq  O(\delta). \]
   647	\end{enumerate}
   648	
   649	\end{theorem}
   650	\begin{proof}
   651	 	A proof of the rigidity of the Magic Square game can be found in~\cite[Theorem 6.9]{coladangelo2017robust}. There are a couple minor differences between their rigidity statement and the one stated here. First, they state that the robustness of the Magic Square self-test is $O(\eps)$; however they specify the closeness between the actual and ideal states in terms of the trace norm, whereas we specify the closeness between $\phi_\alice \otimes \phi_\bob \ket{\psi}$ and $\ket{\EPR_2}^{\otimes 2}\otimes \ket{\aux}$ in terms of the Euclidean distance, which translates to $O(\sqrt{\eps})$ instead of $O(\eps)$. Second, their choice of ideal strategy specifies that the observables corresponding to $\Variable_1$ and $\Variable_5$ questions are $I \otimes \sigma^Z$ and $\sigma^{Z} \sigma^{X} \otimes \sigma^Z \sigma^X$; however under a local change of basis these are equivalent to $\sigma^X \otimes I$ and $\sigma^Z \otimes I$ respectively.
   652	\end{proof}
   653	
   654	We will need the following theorem,
   655	which shows that any pair of anticommuting observables 
   656	can be used to form a value-$1$ strategy for the Magic Square game.
   657

/-!
# The Magic Square game

The Magic Square component is represented by finite constraint and variable
question types, the incidence graph, and the two corresponding answer forms.
Its rigidity theorem is outside the stage-4.1 statement closure; only the game
carrier is needed here.

## References

This file formalizes `def:ms-game` in
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`, from
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
-/

namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT

open MIPStarRE.LDT

/-- A Magic Square question is either a row/column constraint or a cell
variable.  This is `def:ms-game`, blueprint lines 188-203, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
-/
inductive MsType where
  | constraint (i : Fin 6)
  | var (j : Fin 9)
  deriving DecidableEq, Repr, Inhabited, Fintype

/-- The cell incident to a constraint and one of its three positions in
`def:ms-game`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
-/
def msConstraintVars (i : Fin 6) (j : Fin 3) : Fin 9 :=
  ⟨if i.val < 3 then i.val * 3 + j.val else i.val - 3 + j.val * 3, by
    by_cases h : i.val < 3 <;> simp [h] <;> omega⟩

/-- The exceptional Magic Square parity, equal to one only on the final
constraint.  Blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`; paper
origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
-/
def msParity (i : Fin 6) : ZMod 2 :=
  if i.val = 5 then 1 else 0

/-- The 18 constraint-variable incidence edges of the Magic Square graph in
`def:ms-game`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
-/
def msEdges : Finset (Sym2 MsType) :=
  (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin 6 × Fin 3)).image (fun ij =>
    Sym2.mk (.constraint ij.1) (.var (msConstraintVars ij.1 ij.2)))

/-- The Magic Square incidence graph has an edge, as required by the
nonempty-support API of `graphDistribution`.  This is the finite carrier fact
used to instantiate `def:ms-game`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`,
paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
-/
theorem msEdges_nonempty : msEdges.Nonempty := by
  refine ⟨Sym2.mk (.constraint 0) (.var (msConstraintVars 0 0)), ?_⟩
  exact Finset.mem_image.mpr ⟨(0, 0), Finset.mem_univ _, rfl⟩

/-- A Magic Square answer is a parity triple or a single cell bit, as prescribed
by `def:ms-game`, blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`,
paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
-/
inductive MsAnswer where
  | triple (β : Fin 3 → ZMod 2)
  | bit (γ : ZMod 2)
  deriving DecidableEq

/-- A finite code for the two Magic Square answer constructors.  This is
Lean-only carrier infrastructure for `def:ms-game`, blueprint
`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
-/
abbrev MsAnswerCode := (Fin 3 → ZMod 2) ⊕ ZMod 2

/-- The constructor-preserving code equivalence for `MsAnswer`; Lean-only
finite-carrier infrastructure for `def:ms-game`, blueprint
`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
-/
noncomputable def msAnswerEquiv : MsAnswer ≃ MsAnswerCode where
  toFun
    | .triple β => .inl β
    | .bit γ => .inr γ
  invFun
    | .inl β => .triple β
    | .inr γ => .bit γ
  left_inv := by intro x; cases x <;> rfl
  right_inv := by
    intro x
    cases x <;> rfl

noncomputable instance : Fintype MsAnswer :=
  Fintype.ofEquiv MsAnswerCode msAnswerEquiv.symm

instance : Inhabited MsAnswer := ⟨.bit 0⟩

/-- The Magic Square consistency predicate.  Constructor mismatches are
rejected, as required by `def:ms-game` (blueprint lines 188-203; paper
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`).
-/
def msWinPredicate :
    MsType → MsType → MsAnswer → MsAnswer → Bool
  | .constraint i, .constraint j, .triple β, .triple β' =>
      decide (i = j ∧ β = β')
  | .var i, .var j, .bit γ, .bit γ' =>
      decide (i = j ∧ γ = γ')
  | .constraint i, .var j, .triple β, .bit γ =>
      decide
        ((∑ k : Fin 3, β k) = msParity i ∧
          ∃ k : Fin 3, msConstraintVars i k = j ∧ β k = γ)
  | .var j, .constraint i, .bit γ, .triple β =>
      decide
        ((∑ k : Fin 3, β k) = msParity i ∧
          ∃ k : Fin 3, msConstraintVars i k = j ∧ β k = γ)
  | _, _, _, _ => false

/-- The Magic Square game as a finite `Game`.  This is `def:ms-game` in
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
-/
noncomputable def msGame : Game where
  QuestionA := MsType
  QuestionB := MsType
  AnswerA := MsAnswer
  AnswerB := MsAnswer
  μ := graphDistribution msEdges msEdges_nonempty
  μ_prob := by sorry
  decide := msWinPredicate

end MIPStarRE.QPBT

   263	  We say that \emph{$\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{N^x_a\}$ are $\delta$-close on state
   264	    $\ket{\psi}$ and under distribution $\mu$} if
   265	  \begin{equation*}
   266	    \E_{x\sim \mu} \sum_a \norm{ (M^x_a - N^x_a) \ket{\psi} }^2 \leq O(\delta)\;,
   267	  \end{equation*}
   268	  and we write $M^x_a \approx_\delta N^x_a$ to denote this when the state
   269	  $\ket{\psi}$ and distribution $\mu$ are clear from context.
   270	  This distance is referred to as the \emph{state-dependent} distance.
   271	\end{definition}
   272	
   273	\begin{definition}[Distance between strategies]
   274	  \label{def:strategy-distance}
   275	  Let $\game = (\cal{X}, \cal{Y}, \cal{A}, \cal{B}, \mu, D)$ be a nonlocal game
   276	  and let $\strategy = (\psi, A, B)$, $\strategy' = (\psi', A', B')$ be 
   277	  strategies for $\game$.
   278	  For $\delta\in[0,1]$ we say that \emph{$\strategy$ is $\delta$-close to
   279	    $\strategy'$} if the following conditions hold.
   280	  \begin{enumerate}
   281		\item The states $\ket{\psi}, \ket{\psi'}$ are states in the same
   282	    Hilbert space $\mH_A \otimes \mH_B$ and are $\delta$-close.
   283		\item For all $x \in \cal{X}, y \in \cal{Y}$, we have $A^x_a \approx_\delta
   284	    (A')^x_a$ and $B^y_b \approx_\delta (B')^y_b$, with the approximations
   285	    holding under the distribution $\mu$, and on either $\ket{\psi}$ or
   286	    $\ket{\psi'}$.
   287	  \end{enumerate}
   288	\end{definition}

     7	measurements and records the two quantitative consistency statements imported
     8	by the QPBT analysis.

    10	## References
    11

    13	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:357-427`, with paper origin
    14	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:465-525`.

    23	/-- The ordered product
    24	`G^k_{g_k} ... G^1_{g_1} ... G^k_{g_k}` of `lem:ld-sandwich`.
    25	
    26	**Local fix:** The source reverses the outcome indices, which is ill-typed when
    27	the outcome families differ. This definition uses the pairing corrected in
    28	`rem:ld-sandwich-indexing`; blueprint `ch12_qpbt_games.tex:364-391`, paper
    29	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:465-501`.
    30	The empty product is `1`. -/
    31	noncomputable def sandwichProduct {k : ℕ} {X Y ι : Type*}
    32	    [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι] {R : Fin k → Type*}
    33	    (G : (i : Fin k) → X → (Y → R i) → Op ι) (x : X)
    34	    (g : (i : Fin k) → Y → R i) : Op ι :=
    35	  let operators := List.ofFn (fun i : Fin k => G i x (g i))
    36	  operators.reverse.prod * operators.tail.prod
    37	
    38	/-- The two-family sandwiched product
    39	`(G₂)_{g₂} (G₁)_{g₁} (G₂)_{g₂}` from `eq:pasting-2a`; blueprint
    40	`ch12_qpbt_games.tex:402-427`, paper
    41	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:504-525`. -/
    42	def pastedMeasurement {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    43	    {G₁ G₂ : Type*} (M₁ : G₁ → Op ι) (M₂ : G₂ → Op ι)
    44	    (g₁ : G₁) (g₂ : G₂) : Op ι :=
    45	  M₂ g₂ * M₁ g₁ * M₂ g₂

    48	formalization-only auxiliary for `lem:ld-sandwich`, blueprint
    49	`ch12_qpbt_games.tex:364-385`, paper
    50	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:465-495`. -/
    51	def evalFunctionTuple {k : ℕ} {Y : Type*} {R : Fin k → Type*}
    52	    (y : Y) (g : (i : Fin k) → Y → R i) : (i : Fin k) → R i :=
    53	  fun i => g i y
    54	
    55	/-- The sandwiched simultaneous-measurement estimate of `lem:ld-sandwich`.
    56	The universal asymptotic constant is quantified before the distribution,
    57	measurements, state, and error parameters. Blueprint
    58	`ch12_qpbt_games.tex:364-391`, paper
    59	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:465-501`. -/
    60	theorem consistencyDefect_sandwich_le {k : ℕ} {X Y ιA ιB : Type*}
    61	    [Fintype X] [DecidableEq X] [Fintype Y] [DecidableEq Y] [Nonempty Y]
    62	    [Fintype ιA] [DecidableEq ιA] [Fintype ιB] [DecidableEq ιB]
    63	    {R : Fin k → Type*}
    64	    [∀ i, Fintype (R i)] [∀ i, DecidableEq (R i)] :
    65	    ∃ C₀ : ℝ, 1 ≤ C₀ ∧ ∀ (μ : Distribution X)
    66	      (G : (i : Fin k) → X → Measurement (Y → R i) ιB)
    67	      (A : X → Measurement ((i : Fin k) → Y → R i) ιA)
    68	      (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA × ιB)) (ε δ : ℝ),

    70	      (∀ i x, MIPStarRE.QPBT.Measurement.IsProjective (G i x)) →
    71	      (∀ x, MIPStarRE.QPBT.Measurement.IsProjective (A x)) →
    72	      (∀ i (g g' : Y → R i), g ≠ g' →
    73	        avgOver (uniformDistribution Y)
    74	          (fun y => if g y = g' y then 1 else 0) ≤ ε) →
    75	      (∀ i, consistencyDefect (Distribution.prod μ (uniformDistribution Y))
    76	        (fun xy a => heteroKron (((A xy.1).postprocess
    77	          (fun g => g i xy.2)).effect a) 1)
    78	        (fun xy a => heteroKron 1 (((G i xy.1).postprocess
    79	          (fun g => g xy.2)).effect a)) ψ ≤ δ) →
    80	      consistencyDefect (Distribution.prod μ (uniformDistribution Y))
    81	        (fun xy a => heteroKron (((A xy.1).postprocess
    82	          (evalFunctionTuple xy.2)).effect a) 1)
    83	        (fun xy a => heteroKron 1 (∑ g : (i : Fin k) → Y → R i,
    84	          if evalFunctionTuple xy.2 g = a then
    85	            sandwichProduct (fun i x h => (G i x).effect h) xy.1 g else 0)) ψ ≤

    88	
    89	/-- The positive-mass conditional collision bound used by `lem:pasting`.
    90	This is a formalization-only spelling of the conditional probability in
    91	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:394-427`, with paper origin
    92	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:504-525`. -/
    93	def HasConditionalCollisionBound {X Y₁ Y₂ R₂ : Type*}
    94	    [Fintype X] [DecidableEq X] [Fintype Y₁] [DecidableEq Y₁]
    95	    [Fintype Y₂] [DecidableEq Y₂] [Fintype R₂] [DecidableEq R₂]
    96	    (D : Distribution ((X × Y₁) × Y₂)) (G₂ : Finset (Y₂ → R₂))
    97	    (η : ℝ) : Prop :=
    98	  ∀ x y₁, 0 < (D.map Prod.fst).weight (x, y₁) →
    99	    ∀ g ∈ G₂, ∀ g' ∈ G₂, g ≠ g' →

   101	        if g y₂ = g' y₂ then 1 else 0) ≤
   102	        η * (D.map Prod.fst).weight (x, y₁)
   103	
   104	/-- Pasting two consistent measurements yields a polynomially small error.
   105	The output error predicate is the shared two-variable contract, and all
   106	operator families in the conclusion are the postprocessed source families.
   107	This is `lem:pasting`, blueprint `ch12_qpbt_games.tex:402-427`, paper
   108	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:504-525`. -/
   109	theorem exists_pasting_error :
   110	    ∃ δp : ℝ → ℝ → ℝ, IsPolyErr2 δp ∧
   111	      ∀ {X Y₁ Y₂ R₁ R₂ ιA ιB : Type*}
   112	        [Fintype X] [DecidableEq X] [Fintype Y₁] [DecidableEq Y₁]
   113	        [Fintype Y₂] [DecidableEq Y₂] [Fintype R₁] [DecidableEq R₁]
   114	        [Fintype R₂] [DecidableEq R₂]
   115	        [Fintype ιA] [DecidableEq ιA] [Fintype ιB] [DecidableEq ιB]
   116	        (D : Distribution ((X × Y₁) × Y₂))
   117	        (G₁ : X → Measurement (Y₁ → R₁) ιB)
   118	        (G₂ : X → Measurement (Y₂ → R₂) ιB)
   119	        (A : ((X × Y₁) × Y₂) → Measurement (R₁ × R₂) ιA)
   120	        (A' : ((X × Y₁) × Y₂) → Measurement (R₁ × R₂) ιB)
   121	        (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA × ιB)) (η δ : ℝ),
   122	        D.IsProbability → 0 ≤ η → 0 ≤ δ →
   123	        (∀ x, MIPStarRE.QPBT.Measurement.IsProjective (G₂ x)) →
   124	        (∀ q, MIPStarRE.QPBT.Measurement.IsProjective (A q)) →
   125	        (∀ q, MIPStarRE.QPBT.Measurement.IsProjective (A' q)) →
   126	        HasConditionalCollisionBound D (Finset.univ : Finset (Y₂ → R₂)) η →
   127	        consistencyDefect D
   128	          (fun q a₁ => heteroKron (((A q).postprocess Prod.fst).effect a₁) 1)
   129	          (fun q a₁ => heteroKron 1 (((G₁ q.1.1).postprocess
   130	            (fun g => g q.1.2)).effect a₁)) ψ ≤ δ →
   131	        consistencyDefect D
   132	          (fun q a₂ => heteroKron (((A q).postprocess Prod.snd).effect a₂) 1)
   133	          (fun q a₂ => heteroKron 1 (((G₂ q.1.1).postprocess
   134	            (fun g => g q.2)).effect a₂)) ψ ≤ δ →
   135	        consistencyDefect D (fun q a => heteroKron ((A q).effect a) 1)
   136	          (fun q a => heteroKron 1 ((A' q).effect a)) ψ ≤ δ →
   137	        consistencyDefect D (fun q a => heteroKron ((A q).effect a) 1)
   138	          (fun q a => heteroKron 1 (∑ g₁ : Y₁ → R₁, ∑ g₂ : Y₂ → R₂,
   139	            if (g₁ q.1.2, g₂ q.2) = a then
   140	              pastedMeasurement (fun g => (G₁ q.1.1).effect g)
   141	                (fun g => (G₂ q.1.1).effect g) g₁ g₂ else 0)) ψ ≤ δp η δ := by

     5	/-!
     6	# Distribution infrastructure for the low individual degree test
     7	
     8	Shared distribution definitions: finite-support weighted distributions,
     9	a probability predicate, push-forward distributions, weighted-sum linear maps,
    10	averaging, uniform distribution, and outcome summation.
    11	
    12	Note: this module contributes declarations to the comparator statement closure
    13	of `mainFormal`, which must elaborate in the same environment as the
    14	Mathlib-only `Challenge.lean`.  Keep the full `import Mathlib`; do not narrow
    15	it.  See `docs/comparator.md`, "Environment alignment".
    16	-/
    17	
    18	open scoped BigOperators MatrixOrder Matrix ComplexOrder
    19	
    20	namespace MIPStarRE.LDT
    21	
    22	/-- A finite-support weighted distribution with nonnegative real-valued weights. -/
    23	structure Distribution (α : Type*) where
    24	  support : Finset α := ∅
    25	  weight : α → Error := fun _ => 0
    26	  nonnegative : ∀ a, 0 ≤ weight a := by intro _; positivity
    27	  outsideSupport : ∀ a, a ∉ support → weight a = 0 := by intro _ _; rfl
    28	
    29	namespace Distribution
    30	
    31	/-- The total mass carried by the explicit support of a distribution. -/
    32	def totalWeight {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α) : Error :=
    33	  ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a
    34	
    35	/-- A `Distribution` is probabilistic when its total mass is exactly `1`. -/
    36	def IsProbability {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α) : Prop :=
    37	  𝒟.totalWeight = 1
    38	
    39	/-- Push a finite-support distribution forward along a map.
    40	
    41	This is the project `Distribution` analogue of `PMF.map`.  The support is the
    42	image of the original finite support, and each new weight is the sum of the
    43	weights in the corresponding fiber. -/
    44	noncomputable def map {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    45	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) : Distribution β where
    46	  support := 𝒟.support.image e
    47	  weight := fun b => ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support.filter (fun a => e a = b), 𝒟.weight a
    48	  nonnegative := fun _ => Finset.sum_nonneg fun a _ => 𝒟.nonnegative a
    49	  outsideSupport := fun _ hb =>
    50	    Finset.sum_eq_zero fun a ha =>
    51	      (hb (Finset.mem_image.mpr
    52	        ⟨a, (Finset.mem_filter.mp ha).1, (Finset.mem_filter.mp ha).2⟩)).elim
    53	
    54	@[simp]
    55	theorem map_support {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    56	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) :
    57	    (𝒟.map e).support = 𝒟.support.image e := rfl
    58	
    59	@[simp]
    60	theorem map_weight {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    61	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) (b : β) :
    62	    (𝒟.map e).weight b =
    63	      ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support.filter (fun a => e a = b), 𝒟.weight a := rfl
    64	
    65	/-- Push-forward preserves total mass. -/
    66	theorem map_totalWeight {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    67	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) :
    68	    (𝒟.map e).totalWeight = 𝒟.totalWeight := by
    69	  simpa [totalWeight, map] using
    70	    (Finset.sum_fiberwise_of_maps_to
    71	      (s := 𝒟.support) (t := 𝒟.support.image e) (g := e)
    72	      (fun a ha => Finset.mem_image.mpr ⟨a, ha, rfl⟩) 𝒟.weight)
    73	
    74	/-- A finite weighted sum over a push-forward distribution is the corresponding
    75	weighted sum of the pulled-back family.  This is the `Distribution` analogue of
    76	the finite-sum form of `PMF.map`. -/
    77	theorem map_sum_smul {α β M : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    78	    [AddCommMonoid M] [Module Error M]
    79	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) (f : β → M) :
    80	    ∑ b ∈ (𝒟.map e).support, (𝒟.map e).weight b • f b =
    81	      ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a • f (e a) := by
    82	  classical
    83	  calc
    84	    ∑ b ∈ 𝒟.support.image e,
    85	        (∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support.filter (fun a => e a = b), 𝒟.weight a) • f b
    86	        = ∑ b ∈ 𝒟.support.image e,
    87	            ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support.filter (fun a => e a = b), 𝒟.weight a • f (e a) := by
    88	          refine Finset.sum_congr rfl ?_
    89	          intro b _
    90	          rw [Finset.sum_smul]
    91	          refine Finset.sum_congr rfl ?_
    92	          intro a ha
    93	          exact congrArg (fun x => 𝒟.weight a • f x) (Finset.mem_filter.mp ha).2.symm
    94	    _ = ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a • f (e a) := by
    95	          exact Finset.sum_fiberwise_of_maps_to
    96	            (s := 𝒟.support) (t := 𝒟.support.image e) (g := e)
    97	            (fun a ha => Finset.mem_image.mpr ⟨a, ha, rfl⟩)
    98	            (fun a => 𝒟.weight a • f (e a))
    99	
   100	end Distribution
   101	
   102	/-- On a finite ambient type, a summand that vanishes outside a distribution's
   103	explicit support has the same total sum over all ambient values as over that support.
   104	
   105	This is a project-local explicit-support adapter around Mathlib's `Finset.sum_subset`:
   106	Mathlib supplies the finite-sum theorem, while this lemma packages the common shape used
   107	when paper expressions sum over a whole question set but the repository stores a smaller
   108	`Distribution.support`.  It is not intended to replace Mathlib probability theory. -/
   109	theorem Distribution.sum_univ_eq_sum_support {α β : Type*} [Fintype α]
   110	    [AddCommMonoid β] (𝒟 : Distribution α) (f : α → β)
   111	    (hf : ∀ a, a ∉ 𝒟.support → f a = 0) :
   112	    (∑ a : α, f a) = ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, f a := by
   113	  classical
   114	  simpa using
   115	    (Finset.sum_subset (Finset.subset_univ 𝒟.support)
   116	      (fun a _ ha => hf a ha)).symm

   118	namespace Distribution.IsProbability

   120	/-- Unpack the equality form of the probability invariant. -/
   121	theorem weight_sum_eq_one {α : Type*}
   122	    {𝒟 : Distribution α} (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) :
   123	    ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a = 1 := by
   124	  simpa [Distribution.IsProbability, Distribution.totalWeight] using h𝒟
   125	
   126	/-- On a finite ambient type, a probabilistic `Distribution` has total weight `1` even
   127	when its weights are summed over the whole ambient type.
   128	
   129	This packages the explicit-support bookkeeping in `Distribution` for downstream Lean
   130	statements that follow the paper's notation `𝔼_{x ∼ 𝒟}` over the question set rather
   131	than over a stored support finset. -/
   132	theorem weight_sum_univ_eq_one {α : Type*} [Fintype α]
   133	    {𝒟 : Distribution α} (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) :
   134	    (∑ a : α, 𝒟.weight a) = 1 := by
   135	  rw [Distribution.sum_univ_eq_sum_support 𝒟 𝒟.weight 𝒟.outsideSupport]
   136	  exact h𝒟.weight_sum_eq_one
   137	
   138	/-- A probability distribution has total weight at most `1`. -/
   139	theorem weight_sum_le_one {α : Type*}
   140	    {𝒟 : Distribution α} (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) :
   141	    ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a ≤ 1 :=
   142	  le_of_eq h𝒟.weight_sum_eq_one
   143	
   144	/-- Push-forward preserves the probability invariant. -/
   145	theorem map {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
   146	    {𝒟 : Distribution α} (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) (e : α → β) :
   147	    (𝒟.map e).IsProbability := by
   148	  simpa [Distribution.IsProbability, Distribution.map_totalWeight] using h𝒟
   149	
   150	end Distribution.IsProbability

   152	namespace Distribution
   153	
   154	/-- The Mathlib probability mass function associated to a project `Distribution`
   155	whose total mass is one.
   156	
   157	The construction sends each nonnegative real weight to `ℝ≥0∞` by
   158	`ENNReal.ofReal`; the hypotheses of `PMF.ofFinset` are exactly the project
   159	probability invariant and the stored zero-off-support condition. -/
   160	noncomputable def toPMF {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α)
   161	    (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) : PMF α :=
   162	  PMF.ofFinset (fun a => ENNReal.ofReal (𝒟.weight a)) 𝒟.support
   163	    (by
   164	      rw [← ENNReal.ofReal_sum_of_nonneg (fun a _ => 𝒟.nonnegative a),
   165	        h𝒟.weight_sum_eq_one]
   166	      simp)
   167	    (by
   168	      intro a ha
   169	      rw [𝒟.outsideSupport a ha]
   170	      simp)

   172	@[simp]
   173	theorem toPMF_apply {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α)
   174	    (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) (a : α) :
   175	    𝒟.toPMF h𝒟 a = ENNReal.ofReal (𝒟.weight a) := rfl
   176	
   177	@[simp]
   178	theorem toPMF_apply_toReal {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α)
   179	    (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) (a : α) :
   180	    (𝒟.toPMF h𝒟 a).toReal = 𝒟.weight a := by
   181	  rw [toPMF_apply, ENNReal.toReal_ofReal (𝒟.nonnegative a)]
   182	
   183	/-- The associated PMF has zero mass outside the stored support of the project
   184	distribution. -/
   185	theorem toPMF_apply_of_notMem {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α)
   186	    (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) {a : α} (ha : a ∉ 𝒟.support) :

   189	  simp

   192	associated probability mass function. -/

   194	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) (e : α → β) :
   195	    (𝒟.map e).toPMF (h𝒟.map e) = (𝒟.toPMF h𝒟).map e := by

   199	  rw [ENNReal.ofReal_sum_of_nonneg

   201	    (fun a _ => 𝒟.nonnegative a)]

   207	    · have hba : b = e a := hea.symm
   208	      rw [if_pos hea, if_pos hba, toPMF_apply]
   209	    · have hba : b ≠ e a := fun hba => hea hba.symm
   210	      rw [if_neg hea, if_neg hba]
   211	  · intro a ha
   212	    by_cases hba : b = e a
   213	    · rw [if_pos hba, toPMF_apply_of_notMem 𝒟 h𝒟 ha]
   214	    · rw [if_neg hba]

   216	end Distribution

   219	def avgOver {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α) (f : α → Error) : Error :=
   220	  ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a * f a

     3	/-!
     4	# Quantitative state and operator distances
     5	
     6	The blueprint uses asymptotic `approx` notation.  The skeleton records the
     7	corresponding squared norm functionals explicitly, leaving universal-constant
     8	estimates to later proof stages.
     9	
    10	## References
    11	
    12	These are `def:state-distance` and `def:povm-distance` in
    13	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:171-220`; the paper origin is
    14	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:219-271`.
    15	-/
    16	
    17	open scoped BigOperators
    18	
    19	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    20	
    21	open MIPStarRE.LDT
    22	open MIPStarRE.Quantum
    23	
    24	/--
    25	Squared Euclidean distance between pure states.  Blueprint `def:state-distance`
    26	(`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:171-179`), paper origin
    27	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:219-271`.
    28	-/
    29	noncomputable def stateDistSq {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι]
    30	    [DecidableEq ι]
    31	    (ψ φ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) : ℝ :=
    32	  ‖ψ - φ‖ ^ 2
    33	
    34	/--
    35	Average squared state-dependent distance between two operator families.  This
    36	is `def:povm-distance` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:203-210`,
    37	with paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:219-271`.
    38	-/
    39	noncomputable def opFamilyDistSq {X α ι : Type*}
    40	    [Fintype α] [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    41	    (μ : Distribution X) (M N : X → α → Op ι)
    42	    (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) : ℝ :=
    43	  avgOver μ (fun x =>
    44	    ∑ a : α, ‖applyOperatorToState (M x a - N x a) ψ‖ ^ 2)
    45	
    46	end MIPStarRE.QPBT
